input.question: when you're sick, why do symptoms seem worse at night / when trying to sleep?
input.ground_truth: One of the mechanisms at work is the cortisol level. Cortisol is a steroid hormone your body produces, that (among very many other things) suppresses your immune system. But the Cortisol levels vary during the course of a day. As you might have guessed, the concentration of cortisol in your blood decreases during the day and reaches lower levels in the late evening and night. So basically your symptoms get worse, because there is less immunosuppressive Cortisol to fight the inflammation, which leads to more swelling and stronger pain signals being sent.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body is like a house, and when you’re sick, there are little germs trying to make you feel yucky inside your house.

At night, when you’re trying to sleep, your body is working hard to fix the house. It sends out special helpers (like tiny doctors) to fight the germs. These helpers make a little bit more noise and work a bit harder when you’re resting, because you’re not moving around or eating or playing.

That’s why you might feel more achy, sniffly, or have a sore throat at night—it’s because your body is working extra hard to make you better while you sleep! But don’t worry, that means your body is doing a good job fighting the germs.
